newsitem.title: USA: "Buckyballs" bring Nobel Prize to Texas chemists.
newsitem.headline: "Buckyballs" bring Nobel Prize to Texas chemists.

text.p: "Buckyballs" may not sound like great science, but the chance discovery of the revolutionary molecules won two Texas scientists a not-totally-unexpected Nobel Chemistry Prize on Wednesday.
Rice University chemists Robert Curl and Richard Smalley told reporters they knew their work was of such importance that they might one day capture science's biggest prize.

"When we started this work, we never expected to find this (molecule). After we found it and mulled over its implications, we began to hope (for the Nobel)," Curl said. "One was not expecting it but one could always hope."

The two professors, working with fellow chemist Sir Harold Kroto of the University of Sussex in England, discovered in 1985 what turned out to be an entirely new form of carbon in vaporising experiments on the university campus in Houston.

Kroto said by telephone from his office in the University of Sussex in Britain that he was "totally overwhelmed" by the prize. "This is the greatest day of my life. It's fantastic. I'm about to have my first glass of champagne," he said.

At Kroto's urging, Curl and Smalley had been looking for clues to the formation of long chains of carbon atoms found in space when they happened on the strange, soccer ball-shaped molecules that developed when carbon was vaporised, then recondensed.

"It was serendipity in many respects ... we didn't even have any concept that such molecules might actually exist," said Curl. "We made this beautiful symmetric structure just out of chaos. How that happens is still the big mystery."
They playfully named the molecules "buckminsterfullerenes" after Buckminster Fuller, the man who designed geodesic domes. The name is usually shortened to fullerenes, or buckyballs.

Their discovery touched off a virtual revolution in organic chemistry because they were a hitherto unknown third form of carbon, which has provided the base for totally new types of materials. The other known carbon forms were diamond and graphite.

"This buckyball has become effectively a harbinger of what turns out to an infinite new class of materials. We have not yet completely fathomed the long-term impact of this area," Smalley told reporters via a satellite televison hook-up from Hartford, Connecticut, where he was at a chemists' meeting.

He said buckyballs by themselves currently have no practical application because "they are more expensive than gold," but chemical offshoots called "buckytubes" may one day be used in various forms of electrical conductivity because they grow in long, powerful strands.
Curl said some early experiments were under way that may lead to the use of buckyballs as conduits for medicine in the treatment of cancer.
Smalley said he was pleased but still a little awed by the award. "This isn't really real. This a dream," he said.
Curl first heard of their good fortune from a reporter who called him at home. "It was startling, but I managed to hold on to the phone," he said.
Neither said what they were planning to do with their share of the $1.12 million prize.
